opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what drew me in wasn't a job title or a particular piece of the org chart. It was the conversations. Yann and I have talked for years about where AI research is heading, and we've both had this nagging feeling that the field has converged too narrowly. Everyone is scaling language models, and that's produced remarkable things, but language is a thin slice of how intelligence actually works. A child learns an enormous amount about the physical world before saying a single word, mostly by watching, touching, and predicting what happens next.

So when Yann described what he wanted to build, systems that learn world models, that can reason and plan in a grounded way, and that treat vision and perception as foundational rather than a plug-in, it felt like the research I'd been circling my whole career. A lot of my work has been about visual representation learning, and I've always believed that seeing is one of the most important routes to understanding. Here was a chance to pursue that as the central bet, not a side project.

The other part was the spirit of the thing. Yann has always championed openness: open research, open models, sharing ideas with the community. I've seen how much progress comes from that. A startup with that ethos, plus the freedom to take a long-term, contrarian scientific bet without chasing whatever benchmark is trending this quarter, is pretty rare.

And to be honest, there's some risk in it, which I find exciting. If world models turn out to be the right path, and I think there's a good chance they will, then being there early, helping shape both the science and the culture, is something I didn't want to miss. Even if we're wrong about parts of it, we'll learn something important, and the field needs people willing to explore beyond the mainstream.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the startup offered “the freedom to take a long-term, contrarian scientific bet” and a chance to help shape the science and culture, communicating autonomy as a reason the role appealed to Xie.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was that Yann didn't pitch me a job. He pitched me a problem.

When he first talked to me about it, he didn't say "we need someone to run this team" or "we need a chief scientist." He talked about what he thinks is missing from current AI systems: that they don't really understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they don't plan, and scaling text prediction alone won't get you there. Those are things I've been circling for years in my own work, from ConvNeXt to DiT to Cambrian. Visual representation learning, spatial understanding, how models perceive the world rather than just describe it. So when he said the mission is world models and advanced machine intelligence, it felt less like a recruitment and more like someone saying, "You've been working on half of this, come work on the whole thing."

The second thing was the structure he had in mind for my role. He was very clear that he wanted the research to be led by researchers, and that he wanted me to shape the research agenda rather than inherit one. In a big lab you often spend a lot of energy aligning with roadmaps that were set somewhere else. Yann's view was: here's a small, dense group of people, here's a long horizon, now decide what the actual bets are. That kind of ownership is rare, and it's rare at exactly the moment when the field is becoming very product-driven.

The third thing is more personal. I've known Yann for a long time, going back to FAIR. He's one of the few people who is comfortable being contrarian for a decade and then being right. Even if you disagree with him, and I do on some technical specifics, you learn a lot from being in that kind of environment. He's not optimizing for the next benchmark or the next release cycle. He really is asking what the next paradigm is. And he wanted my role to be the person who turns that long-term vision into concrete research directions and real systems, and who keeps a bridge back to academia and to students.

I also appreciated that he didn't try to oversell it. He said, "This might take a long time, and we might be wrong about some of it." For me that honesty was actually more compelling than any grand promise. It told me this was a scientific project first, and a company second.

r001.rationale: He says Yann wanted him to shape the research agenda and decide the group’s research bets, describing that ownership as rare and compelling.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was the opportunity to help shape the research direction from the beginning. A compelling vision gives you a sense of where you want to go, but it also leaves room to question how to get there. That’s the kind of role I find exciting: working on fundamental questions while taking responsibility for turning ideas into something that works.

r001.rationale: The response says he could help shape the research direction and question how to reach the goal, but it does not clearly identify the autonomy to make independent decisions as the reason the vision appealed to him.

sol-6.1.text: What I find compelling is the ambition to build systems that understand the world, can reason about what might happen next, and can use that understanding to plan. From my perspective, that makes perception a central part of intelligence. The exciting part of a role like that would be connecting fundamental research to a larger system, while still having room to question the assumptions and explore.
